summary.text: A binary pulsar is a pulsar that has a companion star, often a white dwarf or another neutron star.
The companion is usually hard to see directly, but it shows itself through tiny shifts in the timing of the pulsar's pulses.
The Hulse-Taylor system's orbital period has kept decreasing, matching Einstein's equations, which predict orbital energy turning into gravitational radiation.

facts.label: Hulse-Taylor pulsar
facts.value: PSR B1913+16, found at Arecibo in 1974

facts.label: Discoverers
facts.value: Joseph Taylor and Russell Hulse, 1993 Nobel Prize

facts.label: Orbital shrinkage
facts.value: About 76 millionths of a second per year

facts.label: Double pulsar
facts.value: PSR J0737-3039, where both stars are pulsars

items.prompt: Astronomers cannot see a pulsar's dim partner. How can they still tell it is there?

options.label: By looking at changes in the timing of the pulses
By listening for the partner's own radio station
By noticing the pulsar changes colour
By measuring the pulsar's temperature from Earth

items.explain: The companion's presence can be deduced from the timing of the pulsar's pulses, which radio telescopes can measure very accurately.

items.prompt: Hulse noticed the rate of pulses rose and fell regularly. What did that suggest?

options.label: The pulsar was switching itself on and off
The pulsar was circling another star at high speed
Earth's atmosphere was changing the signal
The pulsar was slowly running out of fuel

items.explain: Pulses come faster when the pulsar moves toward Earth and slower when it moves away, a Doppler effect from orbiting a nearby star.

items.prompt: Think of the pulses as ticks of a clock. If the ticking spacing shifts as the clock orbits, what is the simplest reading?

options.label: The clock is running out of energy
The clock is getting heavier each tick
The clock's speed toward and away from us is changing
Someone is adjusting the clock from Earth

items.explain: Changes in the ticking indicate changes in the pulsar's speed toward and away from Earth.

items.prompt: What did the slowly shrinking orbit of PSR B1913+16 say about general relativity?

options.label: It disproved Einstein's equations entirely
It showed the stars were not neutron stars
It was caused by friction with space dust
It fit energy leaving as gravitational waves

items.explain: Measurements of the orbital decay were a near perfect match to Einstein's equations, with orbital energy turning into gravitational radiation.

items.prompt: Hulse and Taylor saw the pulses vary and judged the stars were about equally massive. What did they then suppose about the partner?

options.label: It was probably also a neutron star
It was probably a small planet
It was probably an empty patch of space
It was probably a comet

items.explain: Their analysis of the pulse fluctuations suggested equal masses, which led them to think the other object was also a neutron star.

items.prompt: Near the close part of the orbit, the gravitational field is stronger. What happens to the time between pulses?

options.label: It shrinks because time speeds up
It is lengthened because time slows there
It is unchanged because pulses are fixed
It randomly flips between both

items.explain: Where gravity is stronger, the passage of time slows and the time between pulses lengthens.
